disclaimer: Derived from informal conversational tasks with leading prompts and unequal prior knowledge; not a validated psychometric measure or proven optimal learning style.

preferences.analogies: Prefer close everyday/work examples; explicitly map corresponding components and state where analogy breaks.
preferences.visuals: Prefer functional diagrams (state, causal, flow, prerequisites) when useful; do not require decorative visuals.
preferences.feedback: Objective corrections, no sycophancy; tutor should acknowledge ambiguous questions and its own mistakes.
preferences.progress: Practical syllabus, testable mastery gates, hands-on work, spaced retrieval and portable state.

observed_claims.claim: Frequently asks for the purpose, constraints, and rationale behind technical rules before accepting the mechanism.
Often draws on prior experience to build an explanation and can revise a solution when constraints become explicit.
Circuit-breaker terminology was initially confusing; a circuit analogy and familiar API scenario supported a correct subsequent answer.
English time prepositions were often correctly selected while spontaneous phrasing and collocations were less reliable in short meeting updates.
The learner reports that precise diagrams, familiar analogies, and plain language help comprehension.

evidence.description: Asked for the basis of a three-concurrent-jobs limit before implementing a semaphore
Questioned why a thermostat should switch ON/OFF before accepting hysteresis design
Applied hysteresis from thermostat to water-pump levels, using preceding state
Revised simple backup design into version-preserving copies once change-timing constraints were clarified
Initially found CLOSED/OPEN labels counterintuitive and could not infer circuit-breaker behavior
Correctly predicted OPEN prevents external API calls after circuit analogy explanation
Meeting updates used time prepositions correctly but included 'apply the fixing' and unnatural word order
Learner explicitly prefers accurate diagrams and close, plainly worded analogies

unknowns: No controlled finding that concept-first, problem-first or diagrams are universally superior for this learner.
Long-term retention after an independently scheduled multi-day interval has not been measured.
Topic-specific strengths require a fresh diagnostic.
